What a release means here, and what it deliberately leaves alone.

The releasable unit is the repository, because what ships together sits together — one version, everywhere. Every version-bearing file in this repository — the npm packages under `packages/`, the marketplace catalogue and both host plugin manifests at the root, the skills' version chain (docs/skills/versioning.md), and every SDK manifest ADR 0002 puts on this one chain — carries that same version, written by the `extra-files` list below, which is the one authoritative enumeration of them. release-please bumps the root manifest (this repository's own `package.json`), writes the root `CHANGELOG.md`, and tags `v<version>` — the same bare `v*` tags the plugin's releases already carried, which is why the version history continues rather than restarting.

Two things this configuration refuses. The alternative — releasing `packages/archkeep` alone — cannot ship the catalogue or the plugin manifests, because release-please rejects `extra-files` paths that climb out of the release unit (`..` is refused: measured on the 0.4.0 release lane, `packages/archkeep/../../.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` failed with `illegal pathing characters in path`); making the root the unit is the mechanism that lets one release bump everything. And the extension is not a second component — it was once, and the version chain (docs/skills/versioning.md) is what holds the decision: a client that resolves the server out of the workspace pairs with the engine it is released with, and one version makes the pairing visible instead of a matrix to manage.

`pull-request-title-pattern` overrides the default this repository would reject. release-please titles a release pull request `chore${scope}: release${component} ${version}`, where `${scope}` is the target branch — `chore(main): release 0.5.0`. CI runs commitlint on every pull request title, and `main` is not a valid scope, so the release pull request would fail its own required check and could never merge.

The version is never fixed here across releases; the next cut is named one release at a time. A commit whose message carries a `Release-As: <version>` footer forces exactly that version for exactly one release — the strategy reads the newest such note and returns it verbatim (measured against release-please 17.6.0, the version release-please-action v5.0.0 bundles; the config-file `release-as` key upstream deprecated is not used) — and the release after it computes normally again, so the mechanism self-expires behind the tag it cuts. The `prerelease` key is not set on the 0.x line. release-please 17.6.0 (the version release-please-action v5.0.0 bundles) computes the GitHub release's prerelease flag as `config.prerelease && (!!version.preRelease || version.major === 0)` in `manifest.ts`'s release building — with the key set, every 0.x release is flagged as a prerelease on GitHub, which an ordinary 0.x cut is not. The key was added for the rc candidate era and removed when the line returned to 0.x; the historical rc releases (`1.0.0-rc.1`, `1.0.1-rc.1`) remain correctly flagged. When the candidate ladder resumes, re-add `prerelease: true` so rc cuts are flagged — at major 1, only versions carrying a prerelease suffix are affected.
